title: Real and Virtual Images
notes: A real image forms where reflected rays physically converge. It can be projected onto a screen and is commonly inverted for a single concave-mirror image of a real object beyond F.
A virtual image forms where reflected rays only appear to originate when extended backward. It cannot be projected on a screen; a plane mirror forms an upright virtual image behind the mirror.

For a concave mirror, an object beyond F generally gives a real image; an object between pole and F gives a virtual, upright, magnified image. A convex mirror gives a virtual, upright, diminished image for a real object.

Ray test: follow reflected rays forward. If they meet, the image is real; if only backward extensions meet, it is virtual. This geometric test is more reliable than judging whether the image seems behind the mirror.
Example: a shaving mirror used close to the face has the face inside the concave mirror’s focal length, producing an upright virtual magnified image.

A real image is a place where the rays themselves meet, so a screen put there shows the picture. A virtual image is a place where only the backward extensions of diverging rays meet. The eye can see it, but a screen at that place stays dark. A plane mirror's image is virtual.
confusion: Virtual describes ray geometry, not image brightness.

steps: Their extensions meet 20 cm behind the mirror.
A screen behind the mirror receives no rays from this reflection.
The image is upright and the same size.
